title: 48.8% win rate, but still profitable over a 2-year backtest
author: ashishkaloge
selftext:
I forked a strategy someone shared in the Velator AI community and ran a backtest.  
MA, RSI, MACD through six filters like trend strength, volume, funding rate, session timing, direction etc. and an ATR-based stop.

I tested it on daily candles over 2 years, 453 trades, 79% total net return, 10% realized max DD and a PF of 1.52

What caught my eye was the 48.8% win rate. Less than half the trades won but the gains still outweighed the losses. These are backtest results though, not live returns.

Anyone in the community can copy the strategy, change the rules or try it on paper. Exchange trading is still off, but you can receive signals.

What would you like to check next before trusting these results?

replies.body: Yeah, it is shared in the community section on Velator AI. You can copy it from there, check the rules and run your own backtest or try it on paper.

comments.author: legacypogo
comments.body: Waiting for people to provide live results even on seed portfolios or buckets that's more than 500 bucks.  Using AI to invest and the LEFT community need more real, live results to the strategies that people keep backtesting, then go quiet.

replies.author: ashishkaloge
replies.body: fair one. I do not have live results for this one yet. I’ve deployed it on paper, so we can keep track of how it performs. Still not real money, but we will see what happens after a month or so. That should give us more to go on before considering real money.

replies.author: legacypogo
replies.body:
There's nothing wrong with that except the biggest wall in investing is psychology and behaviour.  Paper trading is fine but it doesn't do anything that backtesting doesn't already provide.  The only difference is looking forward vs looking back, neither will cause' real friction in your brain because no skin is in it.

Even many paper traders just disappear.  For every 100 backtests/AI commentary there's maybe 1 person showing any conviction in both communities.  Throw in 1k that you don't mind losing (it's literally the market after all) and let it ride like how AI investing should be or whatever premade LEFT strategy (9sig, 200sma derivative, etc).  If it works scale it.  If it doesn't back to the drawing board or wait it out. The numbers prove them right or at least directionally correct, yet no trigger pulls.

That's ultimately the reality of the retail investor: can you execute the plan or not.

comments.author: Significant_Ball_280
comments.body: That's great but on what stock? MACD, RSI etc are timing tools, not a strategy. They are technical indicators, indicators being the magic word here. They help to indicate when it's a good time to trade the long or short, not whether the stock is any good or not.

comments.author: Careless-Rent-4903
comments.body: 48% win rate isnt a problem at all, with PF 1.5 it means your average winner is roughly 1.6x the average loser. id be more worried about the 6 filters and whether they were chosen using the same 2 years because thats where overfitting usually hides. next id keep a completely untouched period run walk forward and perturb every threshold instead of testing only the best config. engines like vectorbt pro are pretty good for plotting the whole parameter surface so you can see if the result sits on a broad stable area or one lucky point. also test higher fees/slippage/funding and be careful with ATR stops on daily candles since OHLC doesnt tell you which level was touched first inside the bar

comments.author: profittoinvest
comments.body:
48.8% win rate wouldn’t worry me at all with a PF of 1.52. I’d be much more interested in whether that 10% max DD survives a much longer test across different market regimes.

What percentage of the account is actually risked on each trade? That matters a lot here. With roughly 30–35% annualized returns, one violent market regime producing a 20–30% drawdown could wipe out a large part of the accumulated gains, and then the more important question becomes how long the strategy needs to recover its previous equity high — or whether it recovers at all.

I’d definitely push the backtest back to 2020 if the data allows it. That gives you several very different environments: strong bull markets, deep sell-offs, sideways periods and some very sharp regime changes. I’d pay particular attention to those transition periods rather than only the final return.

Then compare it with several months of forward testing. If the live/paper curve behaves similarly to the historical one, that would give me much more confidence than the 2-year result alone.
